title: Chapter 126 — The Life-Buoy
paragraphs: Steering now southeastward by Ahab's leveled steel, and with her progress determined solely by Ahab's level log and line, the Pequod held on her path toward the Equator. Making so long a passage through such unfrequented waters, sighting no ships, and before long pushed sideways by unvarying trade winds over monotonously mild waves — all these seemed the strange calm things that come before some riotous and desperate scene.

At last, as the ship neared the outskirts, so to speak, of the Equatorial fishing-ground, and was sailing past a cluster of rocky islets in the deep darkness before dawn, the watch — then headed by Flask — was startled by a cry so plaintively wild and unearthly — like the half-formed wailing of the ghosts of all Herod's murdered Innocents — that every one of them started out of his daydreams, and for some moments they stood, or sat, or leaned, all listening as if transfixed, like the carved Roman slave, for as long as that wild cry could still be heard. The Christian or civilized part of the crew said it was mermaids, and shuddered; but the pagan harpooners were not frightened. Yet the gray Manxman — the oldest sailor of them all — declared that the wild, thrilling sounds they heard were the voices of men newly drowned in the sea.

Ahab, below in his hammock, heard nothing about this until gray dawn, when he came on deck. Then Flask told him the story, not without hinting at dark meanings. He gave a hollow laugh and explained the wonder like this.

Those rocky islands the ship had passed were home to great numbers of seals, and some young seals that had lost their mothers, or some mothers that had lost their young, must have surfaced near the ship and kept company with her, crying and sobbing with that human-like wail of theirs. But this only disturbed some of the men all the more, because most sailors have a very superstitious feeling about seals, which comes not only from their strange cries when in distress but also from the human look of their round heads and half-intelligent faces as they rise peering out of the water alongside. At sea, under certain conditions, seals have more than once been taken for men.

But the crew's forebodings were destined to receive a most plausible confirmation that morning, in the fate of one of their own. At sunrise this man went from his hammock to his post at the fore-masthead; and whether he was not yet even half awake (for sailors sometimes go aloft while still between sleeping and waking) — whether that was the case with this man, there is now no way of knowing. But however that may be, he had not been long at his perch when a cry was heard — a cry and a rushing sound — and looking up, they saw a falling phantom in the air; and looking down, a little tossing heap of white bubbles in the blue of the sea.

The life-buoy — a long slender cask — was dropped from the stern, where it always hung obedient to a cunning spring; but no hand rose to seize it, and the sun had beaten on this cask so long that it had shrunk, so that it slowly filled, and the parched wood also filled at every pore; and the studded, iron-bound cask followed the sailor to the bottom, as if to give him his pillow, though in truth only a hard one.

And so the first man of the Pequod to climb the mast to look out for the White Whale, on the White Whale's own special ground — that man was swallowed up by the deep. But few, perhaps, thought of that at the time. In fact, in a sense, they were not saddened by this event, at least not as an omen; for they saw it not as a sign of evil to come but as the fulfillment of an evil already foretold. They declared that now they knew why they had heard those wild shrieks the night before. But once again the old Manxman said no.

The lost life-buoy now had to be replaced, and Starbuck was told to see to it. But no cask light enough could be found; and in the feverish eagerness of what seemed to be the approaching crisis of the voyage, all hands were impatient with any work except what bore directly on its final end, whatever that might turn out to be. So they were about to leave the ship's stern without a buoy, when Queequeg, by certain strange signs and innuendoes, hinted a hint about his coffin.
"A life-buoy of a coffin!" cried Starbuck, starting.
"Rather queer, that, I should say," said Stubb.
"It will make a good enough one," said Flask. "The carpenter here can arrange it easily."
"Bring it up; there's nothing else for it," said Starbuck, after a melancholy pause. "Rig it, carpenter; do not look at me so — the coffin, I mean. Do you hear me? Rig it."
"Shall I nail down the lid, then, sir?" moving his hand as if holding a hammer.
"And shall I caulk the seams, sir?" moving his hand as with a caulking-iron.
"And then shall I pay it over with pitch, sir?" moving his hand as if holding a pitch-pot.
"Away! What possesses you? Make a life-buoy of the coffin, and no more. Mr. Stubb, Mr. Flask, come forward with me."

"He goes off in a huff. The whole thing he can stand; it's the parts he balks at. Now, I don't like this. I make a leg for Captain Ahab, and he wears it like a gentleman; but I make a bandbox for Queequeg, and he won't put his head in it. Are all my pains over that coffin to go for nothing? And now I'm ordered to make a life-buoy out of it. It's like turning an old coat inside out; I'm going to bring the flesh to the other side now. I don't like this patching sort of business — I don't like it at all; it's undignified; it's not my place. Let tinkers' brats do the tinkering; we're above them. I like to take on nothing but clean, virgin, fair-and-square mathematical jobs, something that properly begins at the beginning, is at the middle when it's halfway, and comes to an end at the finish; not a cobbler's job, that's at an end in the middle and at the beginning at the end. It's an old woman's trick to be handing out cobbling jobs. Lord! what a fondness all old women have for tinkers. I know an old woman of sixty-five who once ran off with a bald-headed young tinker. And that's why I never would work for lonely old widow women ashore, when I kept my job-shop on the Vineyard; they might have taken it into their lonely old heads to run off with me. But heigh-ho! there are no caps at sea but snow-caps. Let me see. Nail down the lid; caulk the seams; pay it over with pitch; batten them down tight, and hang it by the snap-spring over the ship's stern. Were such things ever done with a coffin before? Some superstitious old carpenters, now, would let themselves be tied up in the rigging before they'd do the job. But I'm made of knotty Aroostook hemlock; I don't budge. Cruppered with a coffin! Sailing around with a graveyard tray! But never mind. We woodworkers make bridal bedsteads and card-tables as well as coffins and hearses. We work by the month, or by the job, or for the profit; it's not for us to ask the why and wherefore of our work, unless it's too confounded cobbling, and then we drop it if we can. Hem! I'll do the job tenderly now. I'll have — let's see — how many are in the ship's company, all told? But I've forgotten. Anyway, I'll have thirty separate life-lines with Turk's-head knots, each three feet long, hanging all around the coffin. Then, if the hull goes down, there'll be thirty lively fellows all fighting over one coffin, a sight not seen very often under the sun! Come, hammer, caulking-iron, pitch-pot and marlinspike! Let's get to it."
